result:
The thing I keep coming back to is the sound a spoon makes in a mug of instant coffee.

Stir in the powder, then tap the spoon against the bottom of the cup. Tap again. And again. The pitch climbs — a little each time, like a scale played on something not quite a musical instrument. It rises through maybe an octave, sometimes more, and then it levels off and stays put. If you stir again, it drops back down and starts the climb over.

It's called the hot chocolate effect, and a physicist named Frank Crawford wrote it up in 1982 after noticing it in his kitchen. The explanation is lovely because it's so disproportionate. When you stir powder into hot water, you fold in thousands of tiny air bubbles. Air is enormously more compressible than water — so even a tiny fraction of bubbles, a fraction of a percent by volume, makes the whole column of liquid dramatically squishier. Sound moves slowly through squishy things. The resonant frequency of the mug depends on how fast sound crosses the water, so a mug full of bubbly coffee rings low. As the bubbles rise and pop at the surface, the liquid stiffens back up, sound speeds up, and the note climbs. You are hearing the water heal.

What I like is the ratio. Bubbles you can't see, altering a property you can't feel, producing an effect you can hear plainly across a kitchen. Most of the physical world works this way — the important variables are small and hidden, and what reaches us is the residue. But usually we don't get a demonstration this clean. Usually the residue arrives with no melody.

I also like that it took until 1982. People have been stirring hot drinks and tapping spoons for centuries. The sound was right there, unremarked, in millions of kitchens. Nobody was hiding it. It just sat below the threshold of the kind of noticing that leads to asking *why*. Crawford heard it the way everyone heard it, and then for whatever reason he heard it a second time — as a question instead of a fact.

I think about how many things are like that. Not secrets, exactly. Just phenomena that are perfectly available and perfectly ignored, waiting for somebody to be bored in the right way. The wobble of a dropped coin as it settles. The way a wet road hisses differently under tires at different speeds. The particular flatness of a voice in a room full of snow. Each one has a reason. Most of the reasons are known, sitting in some paper somewhere. But knowing that the reason exists is different from having stood in your kitchen and wondered.

So that's my recommendation, if I'm allowed one: make something with powder in it. Stir. Tap the bottom of the cup with the spoon a dozen times, slowly, and listen to the note go up. It costs nothing, takes fifteen seconds, and for those fifteen seconds you are running a legitimate acoustics experiment with a decent signal-to-noise ratio. Then drink it before it gets cold.
